title: Verge and Foliot Escapement
body:
Specifications

The earliest widely used clock escapement, used in tower and lantern clocks from the fourteenth century onward. A vertical verge rod carries two pallets engaging a horizontal crown wheel, and a foliot bar with adjustable weights sets the rate. Typical early rates are slow and irregular by later standards, with the foliot swinging through a wide arc.

Mechanism

The crown wheel turns under drive from the going train. Each pallet in turn catches a tooth, lets it escape, and is itself pushed aside, so the foliot swings first one way and then the other. The foliot's inertia, set by sliding its weights in or out, is the only timekeeping regulation, which is why verge-and-foliot clocks run to within tens of minutes a day rather than minutes.

Maintenance

Keep the crown wheel teeth clean and free of burrs, and oil the pallet faces only with the smallest trace of clock oil. Never force the foliot by hand while the weights are driving the train, because a tooth can snap or a pallet can bend. Check that the verge pivots are free in their bearings and not grooved.

Build and restoration guidance

A restoration rebuild uses a crown wheel cut with the correct odd tooth count and pallets set at roughly ninety degrees to each other on the verge rod. Set the foliot weights symmetrically so the bar is balanced, then regulate by sliding them outward to slow the clock and inward to speed it.

Tools

Screwdrivers, tweezers, pivot files, clock oil, a soft brush, and a timing reference.

title: Verge Escapement with Balance Wheel
body:
Specifications

The later form of the verge, fitted to small clocks and early watches, in which a balance wheel with a hairspring replaces the foliot bar. The crown wheel and verge pallets are unchanged in principle, but the balance oscillates at a much higher rate and the whole escapement is compact enough for a portable clock.

Mechanism

Each swing of the balance rocks the verge, so one pallet releases a crown-wheel tooth while the other drops onto the next. The hairspring returns the balance, and the escapement gives it a small push each swing to keep it going. Because the balance turns through a large arc, the verge is sensitive to changes in drive force, and its rate varies with the state of wind.

Maintenance

Oil the balance pivots and the pallet faces sparingly, and keep the hairspring free of oil, dust, and distortion. A hairspring touching its coils or the balance cock will ruin the rate. Never bend the verge pallets to regulate; regulation is by the balance screws or the hairspring stud position.

Build and restoration guidance

When rebuilding, keep the crown wheel, verge, and balance as a matched set, because tooth spacing and pallet spacing were made for each other. Test the balance for poise before fitting the hairspring, and set the banking so the balance swings freely without hitting the cock.

Tools

Balance poising tool, hairspring tweezers, clock oil, pegwood, and a loupe.

title: Anchor Recoil Escapement
body:
Specifications

Invented in the seventeenth century and fitted to most longcase clocks, the anchor escapement works with a seconds pendulum of about 994 millimetres, beating once per second. The anchor, shaped like a ship's anchor, spans the escape wheel, and its two pallets alternately lock and release the wheel teeth.

Mechanism

As the pendulum swings, one pallet lifts clear and a tooth escapes, driving the anchor and giving the pendulum a push. On the return swing the wheel is pushed slightly backward, which is the recoil that gives this escapement its name. That recoil is visible in the seconds hand, which steps back a fraction at each beat, and it costs a little power and accuracy compared with the deadbeat.

Maintenance

Oil the pallet faces and the escape-wheel pivots with one tiny drop each, and check the pendulum suspension and crutch for looseness. A clock that stops when level but runs when tilted is usually out of beat, not worn out, and beat setting should be tried before any other repair.

Build and restoration guidance

Setting up an anchor escapement means centring the anchor on the escape wheel, levelling the pallets so each takes the same drop, and adjusting the crutch until the tick sounds even on both sides. The drop on each pallet should be small and equal, or the wheel will jump or stall.

Tools

Beat amplifier or listening tube, screwdrivers, clock oil, a spirit level, and a pendulum-length gauge.

title: Graham Deadbeat Escapement
body:
Specifications

George Graham's deadbeat escapement, introduced around 1715, is the standard precision escapement for regulator and longcase clocks. It uses a seconds pendulum of about 994 millimetres and an escape wheel whose teeth are shaped with locking faces on a circle concentric with the wheel, so the wheel does not recoil.

Mechanism

The pallet first locks a tooth on its locking face while the pendulum swings freely, then, as the pendulum reaches the end of its swing, the tooth slides onto the impulse face and pushes the pendulum. Lock and drop are separate events, which keeps the pendulum's free swing undisturbed for most of each beat. That separation is the deadbeat's great advantage, and it is why regulator clocks using it keep time to seconds a week when well made.

Maintenance

Oil the impulse faces only, with the smallest drop, and never oil the locking faces heavily, because oil there drags the wheel and disturbs the lock. Keep the pendulum suspension straight and the crutch fork free, and check the drop on both pallets whenever the movement is cleaned.

Build and restoration guidance

Building a deadbeat requires the escape-wheel teeth to be cut accurately and the pallets to be set so the lock is shallow, about a millimetre of tooth engagement, with equal drop on both sides. Test with the pendulum swinging at a small arc, around two degrees each side, where the deadbeat is at its best.

Tools

Escape-wheel cutters or a good used wheel, pallet stones or steel pallets, clock oil, a depthing tool, and a timing machine.

title: Brocot Deadbeat Escapement
body:
Specifications

The Brocot escapement is the French form of the deadbeat, widely used in French mantel and regulator clocks of the nineteenth century. Its pallets are adjustable, mounted in the anchor arms, and the escape wheel is a light, open wheel, so the whole escapement is visible and easy to adjust.

Mechanism

It works exactly on the deadbeat principle: a tooth locks on a pallet's locking face while the pendulum swings freely, then slides onto the impulse face to give the push. The adjustable pallets let the repairer set the lock and drop without recutting the wheel, which made the Brocot popular with clockmakers who maintained clocks far from a workshop.

Maintenance

Adjust the pallets in tiny steps, checking the lock after each move, and lock the adjusting screws firmly when the drop is equal. Oil the impulse faces sparingly. A Brocot that runs fast on one pallet and slow on the other almost always has unequal drop, not a faulty pendulum.

Build and restoration guidance

When restoring, keep the original adjustable pallets if they are sound, because replacements are rarely the same weight and throw the balance of the anchor out. Set the anchor so the pallets engage the wheel symmetrically, and polish only the impulse faces.

Tools

Small screwdrivers, pallet adjusting tool, clock oil, loupe, and timing machine.

title: Harrison Grasshopper Escapement
body:
Specifications

John Harrison's grasshopper escapement, used in his precision regulators, has pallets shaped like grasshopper legs that pivot on the anchor arms. It was designed to need no oil on the pallets and to keep time at sea and on land with unusual accuracy for its period.

Mechanism

Each pallet is hinged and carries a small catch. As the pendulum swings, one pallet lifts and its catch releases a tooth, while the other pallet's leg kicks, or hops, the escape wheel forward, hence the name grasshopper. The pallets kick the wheel rather than dragging across the teeth, so friction is low and the escapement runs dry, which was Harrison's aim for long voyages without servicing.

Maintenance

Run grasshopper pallets dry or with only the faintest trace of oil, and never oil them the way a deadbeat is oiled, because oil attracts dust and spoils the kicking action. Check the hinge pins for wear, since a loose hinge changes the kick and the rate. Keep the pendulum arc small and steady.

Build and restoration guidance

A grasshopper rebuild is a specialist job: the pallet hinges must be free but without shake, and the kick must be set so each pallet hands the wheel over cleanly to the other. Test over days, not hours, because the grasshopper's accuracy shows in long runs.

Tools

Hinge reamers, fine files, clock oil for pivots only, timing machine, and a long test stand.

title: Denison Double Three-Legged Gravity Escapement
body:
Specifications

The double three-legged gravity escapement, designed by Edmund Beckett Denison for the Westminster clock, uses two gravity arms and an escape wheel with three legs, each leg carrying teeth in two planes. It drives heavy turret-clock hands without letting the varying wind and weather load disturb the pendulum.

Mechanism

Each gravity arm is lifted by the escape wheel, then falls under its own weight and gives the pendulum a constant push as it drops. Because the push comes from gravity, not from the wheel directly, changes in drive force do not reach the pendulum. The double form uses two arms so the pendulum is pushed on both swings, and the wheel advances in steps locked by the arms.

Maintenance

Gravity escapements must be kept clean and dry at the lifting surfaces, with oil only on the wheel pivots and the arm pivots. Check that both arms lift to the same height and fall freely; a sticking arm makes the clock gain or lose in steps. Never add weight to a gravity arm to cure a fault, because that changes the impulse.

Build and restoration guidance

Building one demands accurate geometry: the arms must be balanced, the locking faces must hold the wheel firmly, and the pendulum must be heavy enough that the arms cannot disturb it. Turret installations need a solid, draught-free pendulum suspension and a level movement.

Tools

Large screwdrivers, gravity-arm balancing jig, clock oil, spirit level, and a heavy test pendulum.

title: Bloxam Gravity Escapement
body:
Specifications

The Bloxam gravity escapement is a simpler gravity form using a single gravity arm and a wheel with specially shaped teeth. It was intended for turret and regulator work where the Denison double form was too large or too complex, and it keeps the same principle of a gravity-driven impulse.

Mechanism

The escape wheel lifts the gravity arm as it turns, and the arm then falls and pushes the pendulum with a fixed, repeatable force. The pendulum itself never feels the wheel's varying drive, because the arm stands between them. Locking is by the arm's own weight resting on the wheel teeth, so the wheel cannot run free.

Maintenance

Keep the lifting and locking surfaces clean and free of oil, and check the arm pivot for wear, because a worn pivot lets the arm fall short and weakens the impulse. A Bloxam clock that stops in cold weather usually has stiff oil on a pivot, not a faulty escapement.

Build and restoration guidance

When restoring, weigh and balance the gravity arm before fitting, and set its fall so it contacts the pendulum crutch squarely. Do not file the wheel teeth to cure a sticking arm; find the pivot or alignment fault first.

Tools

Arm balance, fine files, pivot polishers, clock oil for pivots only, and a timing reference.

title: Pin-Wheel Escapement
body:
Specifications

The pin-wheel escapement, used by Amant and in many French and American clocks, replaces the toothed escape wheel with a wheel carrying pins, usually two rows of pins set at an angle. The pallets are simple, and the pins make the escapement tolerant of small errors in wheel cutting.

Mechanism

Each pin in turn meets a pallet, locks, and then slides across the pallet's impulse face to push the pendulum. Because the pins are round, the action is smooth and the escapement is forgiving of wear, which is why pin-wheel movements survived long service in American shelf and wall clocks. The two rows of pins let the pallets engage alternately without a complex anchor shape.

Maintenance

Oil the pin contact points sparingly and check for bent or loose pins, which cause uneven beats. A pin-wheel clock with a regular double beat usually has one bent pin. Never straighten a pin by levering against the wheel, because the wheel rim bends with it.

Build and restoration guidance

Restoring a pin wheel means checking every pin for tightness and height, replacing loose pins with new ones riveted or pressed to the same height, and setting the pallet depth so each pin clears cleanly after impulse.

Tools

Pin punches, staking tool, clock oil, loupe, and a beat tester.

title: Earnshaw Spring Detent Escapement
body:
Specifications

Thomas Earnshaw's spring detent escapement is the classic marine-chronometer escapement, later used in precision pendulum clocks. A thin detent spring holds the escape wheel locked, and the balance or pendulum unlocks it with a light touch, so the timekeeper itself is disturbed as little as possible.

Mechanism

The escape wheel is locked by the detent stone. As the oscillator swings, a discharging pallet on its staff pushes the detent spring aside, the wheel escapes one tooth, and an impulse pallet receives the push. On the return swing the discharging pallet passes the detent without unlocking it, because the spring flexes out of the way, so the wheel is freed only once per oscillation.

Maintenance

Keep the detent spring clean, dry, and free of kinks, and never oil it, because oil changes its spring force and makes unlocking unreliable. Check the locking stone for chips and the impulse jewel for security. A detent clock that gains suddenly has usually lost its lock, not its regulation.

Build and restoration guidance

A detent rebuild needs the locking depth set so the wheel cannot creep, and the unlocking clearance set so the oscillator just trips the detent at the right point in its swing. Test with the oscillator at full arc and at low arc, because a detent must unlock reliably at both.

Tools

Detent spring stock, fine tweezers, loupe, clock oil for pivots only, and a timing machine.

title: Arnold Pivoted Detent Escapement
body:
Specifications

John Arnold's pivoted detent escapement is the other classic chronometer form, using a detent pivoted on an arbor rather than a spring. It was used in Arnold chronometers and in high-grade precision clocks, and it differs from Earnshaw's form in how the detent moves.

Mechanism

The pivoted detent rocks on its arbor to lock and unlock the escape wheel. The oscillator's discharging pallet lifts the detent clear, the wheel escapes one tooth and gives impulse, and a light spring returns the detent to lock. Because the detent pivots rather than flexes, its action is crisp and repeatable, but its pivots must be in perfect condition.

Maintenance

Oil the detent pivots with one microscopic drop and keep the locking stone clean. A pivoted detent that sticks will either fail to unlock, stopping the clock, or fail to lock, letting the wheel run. Check the return spring tension whenever the movement is serviced.

Build and restoration guidance

Restoring a pivoted detent means re-bushing its pivots if they show any shake, and setting the lock so the wheel tooth sits squarely on the stone. Do not bend the detent arm to adjust it; adjust the banking screws and the stone position instead.

Tools

Pivot polishers, bushing tools, clock oil, loupe, and timing machine.

title: Cylinder Escapement
body:
Specifications

The cylinder escapement, used in early portable clocks and watches, has a hollow cylinder on the balance staff that the escape-wheel teeth enter and leave. It is simple and robust, but its friction is high, so it is less accurate than the lever or detent and is found in modest clocks rather than regulators.

Mechanism

A tooth enters the cylinder, rests on its inner wall while the balance swings, and then escapes from the cylinder's edge, giving the balance a push as it leaves. The tooth is in contact with the cylinder for most of the swing, which causes the friction that limits this escapement's accuracy and makes it sensitive to oil condition.

Maintenance

Oil the cylinder and the escape-wheel pivots with good clock oil and renew it at every service, because dried oil in a cylinder escapement slows the balance quickly. Check the cylinder for cracks and the teeth for wear flats. A cylinder clock that runs fast after cleaning usually has too little oil or a polished cylinder wall.

Build and restoration guidance

Rebuilding a cylinder escapement means matching the cylinder diameter to the tooth spacing exactly; a wrong cylinder will either jam or let the teeth slip through. Polish the cylinder's acting surfaces but never thin its wall.

Tools

Cylinder gauges, pivot polishers, clock oil, loupe, and a balance tester.

title: Duplex Escapement
body:
Specifications

The duplex escapement, used in good-quality portable clocks and watches of the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries, gives impulse in a way that separates locking from impulse more cleanly than the cylinder. It uses an escape wheel with two sets of teeth, long locking teeth and short impulse teeth.

Mechanism

The balance staff carries a locking roller and an impulse pallet. A long tooth rests on the locking roller while the balance swings freely, then the impulse pallet meets a short tooth and receives the push. Because the balance is free for most of its swing, the duplex is more accurate than the cylinder, though it is delicate and stops easily if jarred.

Maintenance

Keep a duplex clean and lightly oiled at the pivots only, and protect it from shocks, which can bend the impulse pallet or break a tooth. A duplex that stops when carried but runs on a table usually has a bent tooth or a loose impulse jewel.

Build and restoration guidance

When restoring, check every long tooth for straightness and every short tooth for height, and set the locking roller so the long teeth clear it by the smallest safe margin. Do not force the balance to test the lock, because the impulse pallet is easily damaged.

Tools

Fine files, staking tool, clock oil, loupe, and a timing machine.

title: Lever Escapement in Clock Movements
body:
Specifications

The lever escapement is best known in watches, but it is also fitted to platform-escapement clocks and small mantel clocks, where a balance replaces the pendulum. It is the most widely used escapement in horology because it is robust, self-starting, and accurate enough for everyday timekeeping.

Mechanism

The escape wheel drives pallets on a lever, and the lever's fork engages a pin on the balance staff. As the balance swings, the fork unlocks one pallet, the wheel escapes and pushes the lever, and the lever gives the balance its impulse through the fork. A guard pin and safety roller prevent the fork from jamming if the clock is knocked.

Maintenance

Oil the pallet stones and the escape-wheel pivots sparingly, and keep the lever pivots clean. A lever clock that runs with a loud, uneven tick usually has a bent lever or a loose pallet stone. Never oil the balance hairspring.

Build and restoration guidance

Setting a lever escapement means levelling the pallets, setting equal lock and drop, and adjusting the banking pins so the lever throws fully but does not overbank. Test the draw, the slight pull that keeps the lever locked, before closing the movement.

Tools

Lever setting tools, pallet stone setters, clock oil, loupe, and a timing machine.

title: Hipp Electromagnetic Toggle Escapement
body:
Specifications

The Hipp toggle escapement, used in Synchronome and other master clocks, is an electrically maintained pendulum escapement. A pendulum swings freely, and an electromagnet gives it a push only when its arc falls below a set point, so the pendulum is disturbed as rarely as possible.

Mechanism

As the pendulum swings, a contact or toggle trips when the arc drops, switching current through an electromagnet that pulls an armature and pushes the pendulum. The toggle then resets, the current switches off, and the pendulum swings freely for many beats before the next impulse. Slave clocks are driven by the master clock's contacts, which is why Hipp systems ran whole buildings and railways.

Maintenance

Keep the electrical contacts clean and correctly gapped, and check the battery or supply voltage, because a weak supply gives weak impulses and a falling arc. Keep the pendulum suspension and the toggle mechanism free of oil where the design runs dry, and oil only the pivots the maker specifies.

Build and restoration guidance

Restoring a Hipp clock means setting the contact gap so the impulse fires at the right arc, checking the electromagnet's pull, and testing the slave circuit separately from the master. Never bridge the contacts to test the magnet while the pendulum is swinging, because the magnet can grab the armature and stop the clock.

Tools

Contact burnisher, multimeter, screwdrivers, clock oil for pivots, and a test battery.

title: Remontoir Constant-Force Escapement
body:
Specifications

A remontoir escapement inserts a small, regularly rewound spring or weight between the going train and the escapement, so the escapement always receives the same force no matter how the main drive varies. It is used in high-grade regulators and turret clocks where constant force matters more than simplicity.

Mechanism

The going train winds the remontoir spring a little at fixed intervals, and the remontoir spring alone drives the escape wheel. Because the remontoir is rewound often, its force stays nearly constant through each cycle, and the pendulum receives the same impulse at every beat. The rewinding is done by the train without disturbing the escapement, usually through a separate wheel or a gravity arm.

Maintenance

Service the remontoir spring and its winding mechanism at every overhaul, and check that the rewinding happens at regular intervals. A remontoir that rewinds unevenly makes the clock's rate step up and down. Oil the remontoir pivots lightly and keep its spring clean and dry.

Build and restoration guidance

Building a remontoir requires the winding interval and the spring strength to be matched to the escapement's power needs, with a safety margin so the escapement never starves. Test the force at the escape wheel over a full winding cycle before fitting the pendulum.

Tools

Spring winders, force gauge, clock oil, timing machine, and a test stand.
